title: I. Plans For Mitya’s Escape
paragraphs: Five days after the trial, very early, at nine in the morning, Alyosha went to see Katerina Ivanovna. He had a matter of great importance to both of them to discuss, and a message to deliver. She received him in the same room where she had once received Grushenka. In the next room Ivan Fyodorovitch lay unconscious, burning with fever. Right after the scene at the trial, Katerina Ivanovna had had the sick, unconscious man carried to her house. She knew the gossip and the general disapproval were bound to follow, and she took no notice. Two relatives lived with her. One had left for Moscow right after the scene in court; the other had stayed. But if both had gone, she would not have changed her mind. She would still have nursed him and sat by him day and night. Varvinsky and Herzenstube were treating him. The famous doctor had gone back to Moscow and had refused to say how the illness would end. The doctors tried to encourage Katerina Ivanovna and Alyosha, but it was clear they could not yet promise any real hope of recovery.

Alyosha visited his sick brother twice a day. This time, though, he had particularly urgent business. He could see how hard it would be to bring up, and yet he had no time to waste. He had another appointment that same morning that could not be put off, so he had to hurry.
They had been talking for a quarter of an hour. Katerina Ivanovna was pale and worn out, and at the same time in a state of hysterical excitement. She already suspected why Alyosha had come.

“Don’t worry about what he decides,” she told Alyosha, with firm emphasis. “One way or another, he will have to come to it. He must escape. That unhappy man, that hero of honor and principle—I don’t mean him, not Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but the man lying on the other side of that door, who gave himself up for his brother,” Katya added, her eyes flashing, “told me the whole plan of escape long ago. You know he has already begun negotiating.... I’ve told you some of it already.... You see, it will probably happen at the third _étape_ from here, while the prisoners are being marched to Siberia. Oh, that is a long way off yet. Ivan Fyodorovitch has already called on the superintendent of the third _étape_. But we don’t know yet who will command the party, and it’s impossible to find that out so far ahead. Tomorrow, perhaps, I’ll show you the whole plan in detail. Ivan Fyodorovitch left it with me on the eve of the trial, in case it was needed.... That was when—do you remember?—you found us quarreling. He had just gone down the stairs, but I saw you and made him come back. Do you remember? Do you know what we were quarreling about?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha.

“Of course he didn’t tell you. It was that plan of escape. He had explained the main idea to me three days earlier, and we started quarreling over it at once, and we went on for three days. We quarreled because he said that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted, he would get him abroad together with that creature. I was furious at once. I can’t tell you why, I don’t know myself why.... Oh, of course I was furious about that creature, and that she should go abroad with Dmitri, too!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips quivering with anger. “The moment Ivan Fyodorovitch saw I was furious about that woman, he decided I was jealous of Dmitri and still loved him. That is how our first quarrel started. I wouldn’t explain, and I couldn’t ask his forgiveness. I couldn’t bear that such a man could suspect me of still loving that ... when I had told him myself, long before, that I did not love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was only my resentment of that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, on the evening you came, he handed me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh, he saw his illness coming! He said the envelope held the details of the escape, and if he died or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya, and only Mitya. Then he left me money, nearly ten thousand. Those are the banknotes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, when he had heard from someone that Ivan had sent them to be changed. It struck me tremendously that Ivan Fyodorovitch had not given up on saving his brother, and that he trusted me with the plan of escape, even though he was still jealous of me and still sure I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No, you can’t understand how great such self-sacrifice is, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence. But then it came to me that he would take it only as joy at the thought of Mitya being saved (and he certainly would have thought so!). The mere possibility of such an unjust thought in his head made me so angry that I lost my temper again. Instead of kissing his feet, I flew into a rage again! Oh, I am unhappy! It’s my character, my awful, unhappy character! Oh, you’ll see, I will end by driving him away, too, for another woman he can get on with better, as Dmitri did. But ... no, I couldn’t bear it, I would kill myself. And when you came in then, and I called out to you and told him to come back, the look of contempt and hatred he gave me enraged me so much that—do you remember?—I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who had convinced me his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to hurt him again. He had never, never convinced me that his brother was a murderer. On the contrary, it was I who convinced him! Oh, my vile temper caused everything! I paved the way for that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to prove to me that he was an honorable man, and that even if I loved his brother, he would not destroy him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court ... I am the cause of it all, I alone am to blame!”

Katya had never made such confessions to Alyosha before. He felt she had reached the point of unbearable suffering where even the proudest heart painfully crushes its own pride and collapses, beaten by grief. Oh, Alyosha knew of another terrible cause of her misery. She had been careful to hide it from him in the days since the trial. For some reason it would have hurt him too much to see her brought so low that she spoke of it now. She was suffering over her “treachery” at the trial. Alyosha felt that her conscience was driving her to confess it to him, to him, Alyosha, with tears and screams and hysterical writhing on the floor. He dreaded that moment and longed to spare her. It made his errand harder still. He spoke of Mitya again.

“It’s all right, it’s all right, don’t be anxious about him!” she started again, sharp and stubborn. “All of that is only for the moment. I know him, I know his heart only too well. You can be certain he will agree to escape. It won’t be right away, after all. He will have time to get used to the idea. Ivan Fyodorovitch will be well by then, and he’ll arrange it all himself, so I’ll have nothing to do with it. Don’t be anxious. He will agree to run away. He has agreed already. Do you think he would give up that creature? And they won’t let her visit him, so he has to escape. It’s you he’s most afraid of. He’s afraid you won’t approve of his escaping, on moral grounds. But you must generously _allow_ it, if your blessing matters so much,” Katya added spitefully. She paused and smiled.

“He talks about some hymn,” she went on, “some cross he has to carry, some duty. I remember Ivan Fyodorovitch told me a great deal about it, and if you knew how he talked!” Katya cried suddenly, with a feeling she could not hold back. “If you knew how much he loved that wretched man when he told me, and how much he hated him, perhaps, in that same moment. And I listened to his story and his tears with a sneer of contempt. Brute! Yes, I am a brute. His fever is my fault. But that man in prison can’t suffer,” Katya finished irritably. “Can a man like that suffer? Men like him never suffer!”

Her words carried hatred and a contemptuous revulsion. And yet she was the one who had betrayed him. “Perhaps she hates him at moments because she knows how she has wronged him,” Alyosha thought to himself. He hoped it was only “at moments.” In Katya’s last words he heard a challenge, but he did not take it up.

“I sent for you this morning so that you would promise to persuade him yourself. Or do you, too, think that escaping would be dishonorable, cowardly, or ... unchristian, maybe?” Katya added, still more defiantly.

“Oh, no. I’ll tell him everything,” Alyosha muttered. “He asks you to come and see him today,” he blurted out suddenly, looking her straight in the face. She started and moved back a little from him on the sofa.
“Me? Is that possible?” she faltered, turning pale.

“It can be, and it ought to be!” Alyosha began forcefully, growing more animated. “He needs you very much just now. I wouldn’t have brought it up and upset you if it weren’t necessary. He is ill, he is beside himself, and he keeps asking for you. He doesn’t want you so that he can make peace with you. He only wants you to come and show yourself at his door. So much has happened to him since that day. He understands that he has wronged you beyond measure. He doesn’t ask your forgiveness—‘It’s impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself—he only asks that you appear in his doorway.”
“It’s so sudden....” Katya faltered. “All these days I’ve had a feeling you would come with this message. I knew he would ask me to come. It’s impossible!”

“Then let it be impossible, but do it. Think of it: for the first time he understands how he has hurt you, the first time in his whole life. He never grasped it so fully before. He said, ‘If she refuses to come, I will be unhappy for the rest of my life.’ Do you hear? He has been sentenced to twenty years of penal servitude, and he is still planning to be happy. Isn’t that pitiful? Think, and you must go to him. He is ruined, but he is innocent,” Alyosha said, and it broke from him like a challenge. “His hands are clean, there is no blood on them! For the sake of the endless suffering waiting for him, go to him now. Go and see him off on his way into the darkness—just stand at his door, that is all.... You ought to do it, you ought to!” Alyosha ended, putting enormous stress on the word “ought.”
“I ought to ... but I cannot....” Katya moaned. “He will look at me.... I can’t.”
“Your eyes ought to meet. How will you live the rest of your life, if you don’t make up your mind to do it now?”
“Better to suffer all my life.”
“You ought to go, you ought to go,” Alyosha said again, with merciless emphasis.
“But why today, why right now?... I can’t leave our patient—”
“You can, for a moment. It will be only a moment. If you don’t come, he will be raving by tonight. I wouldn’t lie to you. Have pity on him!”
“Have pity on _me!_” Katya said, bitterly reproachful, and she burst into tears.
“So you will come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you’re coming right away.”
“No, don’t tell him that, not for anything,” Katya cried in alarm. “I will come, but don’t tell him beforehand. Maybe I will go, and not go in.... I don’t know yet—”
Her voice failed her. She gasped for breath. Alyosha stood up to leave.
“And what if I meet someone?” she said suddenly, in a low voice, turning white again.
“That is exactly why you must go now, so you won’t meet anyone. There will be nobody there, I can tell you that for certain. We will be expecting you,” he concluded firmly, and left the room.
